source_caption:
Whose God belongs in a public classroom? 

That's the question Sheriff Hassan (Rahul Kohli) poses to Bev Keane (Samantha Sloyan) in this unforgettable exchange from Midnight Mass. What begins as a seemingly bureaucratic dispute over distributing the King James Bible in a public school quickly peels back to reveal a raw, systemic power struggle. Bev weaponizes "tradition" and the town’s majority faith to position Christianity as the baseline standard, painting Sheriff Hassan’s concerns as an aggressive, outside attack. By doing so, she illustrates exactly how easily a dominant worldview can be used to marginalize others under the guise of benevolence.

This moment is especially striking because it gives us one of television's most nuanced portrayals of Muslim faith. Hassan doesn't just defend his beliefs, he explains them with patience and dignity. We see how Islam reveres Jesus, how the Quran is understood as a continuation of earlier revelations, and how tolerance should cut both ways. Because if handing out Qurans would be unacceptable, why is distributing Bibles in public schools considered harmless?

Midnight Mass is a masterclass in how easily religious devotion can be weaponized when mixed with isolation and human desperation. Mike Flanagan expertly uses the supernatural element the "vampire" framed as a biblical angel to mirror how real-world communities can rationalize horrific acts under the guise of divine will.The horror of the series doesn't stem from the monster itself, but from the seductive nature of blind faith and the speed with which a community can succumb to religious extremism.

source_details.synopsis: Midnight Mass is an American gothic supernatural horror television miniseries created and directed by Mike Flanagan and starring Zach Gilford, Kate Siegel, Hamish Linklater, Samantha Sloyan, Rahul Kohli, Kristin Lehman, and Henry Thomas. The plot centers on a devout and impoverished Catholic island community that experiences supernatural events after the arrival of a mysterious priest. The series was announced in July 2019, with Netflix ordered Flanagan's original horror series Midnight Mass as part of that overall deal. Flanagan wrote, directed and served as showrunner on the seven-episode series, which suffered from a production delay in 2020 caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Midnight Mass
